<title>Wallet-confirmed OAuth consent — Phase C: push-to-approve with mandatory number matching</title>
<description>
Phase C of `docs/design-plans/2026-07-18-wallet-confirmed-oauth-consent.md`: the convenience layer once the E2E-encrypted notification relay (<issue id="b95fcd23-95fa-43f6-86a6-81defb9dda77" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-311/e2e-encrypted-notification-relay-for-self-hosted-custos-apns">MM-311</issue>) lands. Push adds only a **delivery path** onto the Phase A primitive (<issue id="9cfb3005-9011-4b73-bf18-43ecacfd64ce" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-441/wallet-confirmed-oauth-consent-phase-a-pending-authorization-primitive">MM-441</issue>) — nothing about the pending request, the signed envelope, or the completion path changes.

* Custos seals the relay design's exact `login-approval` payload `{type, request_id, client_name, origin, code}` to the device (`docs/design-plans/2026-07-10-notification-relay.md`); the wallet deep-links into the existing approval screen.
* **Number matching is mandatory on this channel** (it is the anti-MFA-fatigue mitigation for wallet-notified prompts, redundant on the wallet-initiated channels): the consent page displays a short number for push-delivered prompts and the wallet requires the user to enter/confirm it before the biometric gate, alongside origin display.
* Open UX decision (from the design doc): type-the-number (GitHub style, stronger against guess-taps) vs select-from-three (Microsoft style) — decide with the push UX work.

## Acceptance criteria

* A login started on another device produces a push; approval requires the matching number + biometric; a wrong number cannot approve.
* The relay never learns a login is happening (payload sealed; opaque push handle), consistent with the relay's metadata-minimization goals.
* Push delivery failure degrades cleanly to the Phase A/B channels on the same pending request.
</description>

<title>Passwordless auth: retire the account password in favor of device-key/passkey factors</title>
<description>
Follow-up to the passwordless design exploration captured in `docs/design-plans/2026-07-12-passwordless-auth.md` (branch `claude/passwordless-login-bc4umw`).

## Why

The password is already a second-class credential in this architecture: the wallet logs in via OAuth+DPoP and retains no password, the root of trust is the Secure-Enclave device key holding `rotationKeys[0]`, `accounts.password_hash` has been nullable since V008, and `createSession` already falls through to app-password verification for accounts with a NULL main password. Meanwhile password reset is dead in practice (outbound email is stubbed, <issue id="fbeb902e-c32b-400a-af47-37eccd58d65b" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-211/outbound-email-delivery-email-confirmationupdate-endpoints">MM-211</issue>), so the password is an unrecoverable liability posing as a recovery factor. Identity recovery never depended on it — that's the device key's 2-of-3 Shamir split.

## What the password still gates (the actual work)

1. **OAuth consent** (`oauth_authorize.rs`) — the wallet's own login path; a NULL-hash account cannot pass consent today. Needs a device-key-signed or passkey (WebAuthn) factor. The signed-envelope verification pattern already exists for admin-companion devices (`auth/guards.rs::verify_admin_device_request`).
2. **Account creation** — non-empty password required in `/v1/dids` and `createAccount` new-account mode; make optional (migration mode already stores NULL).
3. `deleteAccount` — password + email token in body; rework to email-token-or-wallet-signature for passwordless accounts.
4. Third-party clients (Bluesky app, goat) keep working via **app passwords** minted in the wallet — zero server changes needed.

## Phasing (from the design plan)

* **Phase 1:** optional password at creation; device-key/passkey factor on OAuth consent; `deleteAccount` rework. Keep interop endpoints (password branch of `createSession`, standard `createAccount`) for migrated-in accounts.
* **Phase 2:** cross-device login approval — QR-scan (wallet-initiated, phishing-resistant) first; **push-to-approve** later, once the E2E-encrypted notification relay lands (<pull-request id="34230e45-6259-4c9a-b58d-6b135adf84e3" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/review/design-exploration-e2e-encrypted-notification-relay-for-self-hosted-327f880332d1">malpercio-dev/ezpds#207</pull-request>, `docs/design-plans/2026-07-10-notification-relay.md`). Push-approve needs MFA-fatigue mitigations (origin display, number matching).
* **Hard prerequisite (parallel):** the Shamir reconstruction ceremony (or iCloud-synced passkeys), so a lost device is not a total PDS lockout before the password escape hatch is removed.

## Definition of done (exploration → plan promotion)

* Full design plan with acceptance criteria promoted from the exploration doc
* Decision recorded: passkey/WebAuthn vs device-key-signed consent as the primary factor
* Recovery-ceremony dependency scheduled ahead of any password removal
</description>

# Linear Development Workflow

This skill manages the full lifecycle of working on a Linear issue: from picking it up through opening a PR.

## Starting Work on an Issue

When the user indicates they want to work on a Linear issue (e.g., "Let's work on MM-42"):

1. **Parse the issue identifier** from the user's message. The pattern is `MM-` followed by a number.

2. **Fetch the issue details** from Linear using the `get_issue` tool with the parsed identifier. Display a brief summary to the user: title, description (truncated if long), priority, and any existing labels.

3. **Update the issue in Linear:**
   - Set the status to **"In Progress"**
   - Assign it to **"me"** (the authenticated user)

   Use the `save_issue` tool with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Progress"`, and `assignee: "me"`.

4. **Create a git branch from a fresh base** using the issue's suggested branch name:
   - The `get_issue` response includes a `branchName` field — use that as the branch name.
   - **Fetch first, then branch from the remote tip — never from a possibly-stale local HEAD:**
     `git fetch origin main && git checkout -b <branchName> origin/main`
     A stale base silently duplicates work that already merged (hours lost rebuilding an already-shipped backend is the known failure mode).
   - If the branch already exists locally, check it out, then run `git log --oneline <branchName>..origin/main` and surface to the user how far behind the base is.

5. **Verify sibling work is in the base.** If the issue depends on or overlaps sibling issues already marked Done in Linear, confirm their PRs are actually present in the branch base (e.g. `git log --oneline origin/main | grep -i mm-nnn`, or check for the files/routes they added) before concluding any related feature is "missing". **"Linear says Done but the code isn't here" is a hard stop-and-verify signal — it almost always means your base is stale, not that the feature needs building.**

6. **Confirm to the user** what happened: issue assigned, status updated, branch created/checked out (and from which base commit). Then ask what they'd like to tackle first, or summarize the issue so they can dive in.

## Opening a PR (Auto-transition to "In Review")

When the user asks to open a PR, create a pull request, or you detect that a PR is being created for a branch associated with a Linear issue:

1. **Identify the Linear issue** from the current branch name. Linear branch names typically contain the issue identifier (e.g., `malpercio/mm-42-fix-the-thing`). Extract the `MM-XXX` portion.

2. **Create the PR** as the user requests (follow normal PR creation workflow).

3. **After the PR is successfully created**, update the Linear issue:
   - Set the status to **"In Review"**
   - Attach the PR URL as a link on the issue using the `links` field in `save_issue`

   Use `save_issue` with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Review"`, and `links: [{"url": "<pr-url>", "title": "Pull Request"}]`.

4. **Confirm** to the user that the issue has been moved to "In Review" and the PR link has been attached.

## Important Notes

- Always fetch the issue first to confirm it exists and get the full `id` (UUID) needed for updates.
- If the issue is already "In Progress" and assigned, skip those updates and just create the branch.
- If branch creation fails (e.g., uncommitted changes), inform the user and suggest next steps rather than silently failing.
- The PR-to-"In Review" transition should happen automatically whenever a PR is opened during a session where the user started work on a Linear issue. Track the active issue identifier throughout the session.

1	# Wallet-Confirmed OAuth Consent (Passwordless Sign-In to OAuth Apps)
2	
3	Status: **design exploration** — extends the passwordless-auth exploration
4	([2026-07-12-passwordless-auth.md](2026-07-12-passwordless-auth.md), MM-312) by deciding
5	the concrete cross-device mechanism it left open: device-code entry (Netflix-style) vs
6	number matching (GitHub-style) vs QR vs push. Captures the discussion of 2026-07-18.
7	Implementation tracked as sub-issues of MM-312:
8	[MM-441](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-441) (Phase A),
9	[MM-442](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-442) (Phase B),
10	[MM-443](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-443) (Phase C).
11	
12	## Problem
13	
14	A sovereign account cannot sign in to OAuth apps at all. The consent handler maps a NULL
15	or empty `password_hash` unconditionally to `WrongPassword`
16	(`crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_authorize.rs:560-564`, covered by
17	`post_approve_with_mobile_account_rerenders_consent_page`), and wallet-created /
18	migrated-in accounts store NULL by design (MM-306). So the account that *most* embodies
19	the product's identity model is the one locked out of the ATProto OAuth app ecosystem.
20	There is no push infrastructure yet, but the design must leave a clean slot for it
21	(notification relay, MM-311).
22	
23	## The framing: one primitive, several channels
24	
25	"Device code vs number matching" is not an architecture choice — it is a choice of
26	**discovery channel** onto a single server-side primitive. Decide the primitive once, and
27	every channel (typed code, same-device handoff, QR, push) becomes a thin variant:
28	
29	> **Pending authorization request** — created by the consent page in place of the
30	> password check; approved out-of-band by the wallet with a device-key-signed envelope;
31	> observed by the consent page until it can complete the normal redirect.
32	
33	Nearly all of this already exists in the tree:
34	
35	| Piece | Existing machinery |
36	|---|---|
37	| Pending-request state machine + "approved elsewhere" polling | agent claim ceremony: `agent_claim_attempts` (V037/V038), `routes/oauth_token/claim_polling.rs` (`authorization_pending` / `slow_down` / success, poll throttling, race re-read) |
38	| Passwordless approval credential | sovereign session: `routes/sovereign_session.rs` — canonical envelope signed by a key in the account's **authoritative PLC `rotationKeys`**, nonce anti-replay, timestamp window |
39	| Canonical signed-envelope pattern | ADR-0018 admin envelope (`auth/guards.rs::verify_admin_device_request`, `apps/admin-companion/src-tauri/src/signing.rs`) |
40	| Wallet approval UX (enter code → preview grants → biometric → confirm) | `AgentClaimApprovalScreen.svelte` + `agents.rs` IPC (claim-preview / claim-confirm) |
41	| Consent page + per-scope checkboxes | `oauth_templates.rs::render_consent_page`, MM-237 scope reduction |
42	| Push envelope for a future `login-approval` type | notification relay design ([2026-07-10-notification-relay.md](2026-07-10-notification-relay.md)) already names `{type: "login-approval", request_id, client_name, origin, code}` |
43	
44	The genuinely new pieces are one table, one approval route, one status route, a second
45	path through `oauth_authorize.rs`, and one wallet screen variant.
46	
47	## Channel analysis
48	
49	The security-relevant property is **who carries the binding between the login surface and
50	the wallet**:
51	
52	- **Wallet-initiated** channels (user types a code from the page into the wallet, taps a
53	  link on the page, or scans the page's QR): the *user* carries the binding from the
54	  thing they are logging into. Blind approval is impossible — the wallet has nothing to
55	  show until the user brings it a request.
56	- **Wallet-notified** channels (push, or the wallet polling for pending requests): the
57	  request finds the user. This is where MFA-fatigue / blind-tap attacks live, and where
58	  **number matching** earns its keep — it forces the approver to prove they can see the
59	  login surface.
60	
61	| Channel | Needs push? | Same-device? | Camera? | Phishing profile |
62	|---|---|---|---|---|
63	| Typed short code (Netflix) | no | yes (clunky but works) | no | RFC 8628-style code phishing: attacker starts a login, socially engineers the victim into entering the attacker's code. Mitigated by the wallet preview (client, origin, scopes) before biometric confirm |
64	| Same-device handoff (link on consent page opens wallet with `request_id`) | no | **the** same-device answer | no | same as typed code, minus transcription |
65	| QR scan (page shows QR of `request_id` + origin) | no | no (can't scan own screen) | yes | strongest cross-device: user starts from the page, no transcription, wallet verifies origin from the request server-side |
66	| Push + number match (GitHub/MS Authenticator) | **yes** (MM-311) | yes | no | blind-tap risk is the failure mode; number matching + origin display are the standard mitigations |
67	
68	Two observations that settle the ordering:
69	
70	1. **Number matching is a mitigation for the push channel, not an alternative to the
71	   code.** In every wallet-initiated channel it is redundant — the user already carried
72	   the binding. Building GitHub-style matching *without* push would require the wallet to
73	   discover pending requests by polling, which in turn requires the consent page to
74	   pre-bind a typed handle to the request. That creates an unauthenticated surface where
75	   anyone typing a victim's handle at any Custos consent page makes a prompt appear in
76	   the victim's wallet — importing the MFA-fatigue problem *before* gaining push's
77	   convenience. Rejected as a v1.
78	2. **Same-device is the common case for a mobile-only PDS** (the OAuth client app is on
79	   the same phone as the wallet), and it is exactly the case QR cannot serve. The typed
80	   code always works as the universal fallback (no camera, no push, accessibility-safe,
81	   cross-device and same-device alike) — which is why it ships first.
82	
83	## Shape
84	
85	### The pending request
86	
87	New table (name illustrative) `pending_oauth_authorizations`:
88	
89	- `request_id` (random, high-entropy — used in QR / handoff link / push payload)
90	- `user_code` (short, human-typeable, e.g. 8 chars grouped — the Netflix path; formatted
91	  distinctly from the agent claim code and the operator claim code; ADR-0026 already
92	  warns these "share a word, not a mechanism")
93	- client_id + resolved client metadata snapshot, requested scopes, PAR linkage
94	- requesting origin/IP/user-agent (for wallet display)
95	- optional `login_hint` DID (pre-bound account, if the client supplied one)
96	- status: `pending` / `approved` / `denied` / `expired`; granted-scope set on approval
97	- created/expires (~5 min), single-use
98	
99	### Consent-page flow (`oauth_authorize.rs`, second path)
100	
101	1. `GET /oauth/authorize` for a passwordless-capable flow renders the wallet path
102	   (alongside the password form while passworded accounts exist): creates the pending
103	   request, shows the `user_code`, an "Open in Obsign" handoff link carrying
104	   `request_id` (Phase A), and later a QR (Phase B).
105	2. The page observes `GET /oauth/authorize/status?request_id=…` (JS poll with the same
106	   `slow_down` throttling discipline as `claim_polling.rs`; no-JS fallback: an
107	   "I've approved — continue" button).
108	3. On `approved`, the page completes through the **existing** tail of
109	   `post_authorization`: scope reduction already decided, `store_authorization_code`,
110	   303 to `redirect_uri?code=…&state=…&iss=…`. The token endpoint (PKCE + DPoP) is
111	   untouched.
112	
113	### Wallet approval
114	
115	Reuses the agent-claim screen shape: enter code (or arrive via handoff/QR/push with
116	`request_id`) → **preview** (client name, origin, requesting IP/geo, scope list —
117	reusing the scope-preview treatment from `AgentClaimApprovalScreen.svelte`, and the
118	per-scope uncheck moves here: the wallet is the trusted UI for this path, so the granted
119	set is chosen in the wallet, not on the page) → biometric gate → sign → submit.
120	
121	Approval credential: a **device-key-signed canonical envelope** in the
122	`sovereign_session.rs` mold — domain-versioned string binding server DID, account DID,
123	signing key, `request_id`, `client_id`, a hash of the granted scope set, timestamp,
124	nonce; verified against the **authoritative current PLC `rotationKeys`** (same
125	authoritative-fetch discipline, same nonce anti-replay pattern). This keeps consent
126	strictly key-sovereign: the thing that can approve a login is the thing that owns the
127	identity, sessions optional. (The alternative — authenticate the approval route with
128	`authenticate_account_owner` and skip the envelope — is less code but binds approval to
129	session state instead of the key; the envelope also gives per-approval non-repudiation
130	for the audit log.) Passkeys/WebAuthn remain the complementary *browser-native* factor
131	from the MM-312 open question — additive later, not a competitor to this path.
132	
133	Account binding: if the request carries a `login_hint`, the approving wallet's DID must
134	match. Otherwise the approving wallet binds its DID at approval time (exactly like the
135	agent claim confirm), and the wallet screen states it explicitly: "Sign in to
136	**{client}** at **{origin}** as **@{handle}**".
137	
138	### The push slot (Phase C, after MM-311)
139	
140	Push adds only a delivery path: Custos seals `{type: "login-approval", request_id,
141	client_name, origin, code}` to the device (the relay design's exact payload), the wallet
142	deep-links into the same approval screen — with **number matching now mandatory**: the
143	consent page displays a 2-digit number for push-delivered prompts and the wallet requires
144	the user to enter/select it before the biometric gate, plus origin display. Nothing about
145	the primitive, the envelope, or the completion path changes.
146	
147	## Suggested phasing
148	
149	- **Phase A — code + handoff (no push, no camera).** The pending-request table/routes,
150	  the second consent-page path, typed `user_code` entry in the wallet (clone of the
151	  agent-claim screen), the same-device handoff link. Depends on nothing unbuilt.
152	  **Landed (2026-07-18):** `pending_oauth_authorizations` + `oauth_consent_audit_events`
153	  (V056), `crypto::encode_oauth_consent_envelope` (+ shared golden vector), the
154	  `routes/oauth_consent.rs` routes (wallet preview, `slow_down`-throttled status poll,
155	  device-key-signed approve/deny against authoritative PLC `rotationKeys`, browser
156	  completion through the existing code-issuance tail), the wallet path on the consent page,
157	  and the wallet's `oauth_consent.rs` IPC + `OAuthConsentApprovalScreen`. The signed
158	  envelope binds `request_id` + `client_id` + decision + granted-scope hash; single-use is
159	  enforced by the guarded status transitions (which, with the `request_id` binding, subsume
160	  a nonce store — no separate nonce table). Handoff link degrades to copy-the-code (the
161	  wallet has no deep-link handler yet, per ADR-0006).
162	- **Phase B — QR.** Encode `request_id` + origin on the consent page; wallet scan screen
163	  feeding the same approval flow. Camera plumbing is the only new work.
164	  **Landed (2026-07-19):** the consent page renders an inline-SVG QR (`qrcodegen` →
165	  `render_qr_svg` in `oauth_templates.rs`) encoding the wallet's private-use handoff URI
166	  (`org.obsign.identitywallet:/consent?request_id=…&origin=…`) beside the typed `user_code`, which
167	  stays rendered as the no-camera / accessibility fallback; the same URI backs both the QR and the
168	  same-device "Open in Obsign" link. The wallet gains a `preview_oauth_consent_by_request_id` IPC
169	  command (the server's preview endpoint already resolved by `request_id`) and a camera scan screen
170	  on `OAuthConsentApprovalScreen` via `@tauri-apps/plugin-barcode-scanner` (mobile-only, `#[cfg(mobile)]`,
171	  `NSCameraUsageDescription`, `barcode-scanner:default`). The scan path extracts **only** the
172	  `request_id` from the QR (`parseConsentQr`) and re-verifies it server-side — the client/origin/scope
173	  the wallet displays always come from the server's record, never the QR — then feeds the identical
174	  preview → biometric → device-key-signed-envelope flow. No server protocol change beyond encoding
175	  the QR payload.
176	- **Phase C — push + number matching.** After the notification relay (MM-311) lands:
177	  `login-approval` notification type, deep-link approve/deny, number-match UX.
178	
179	Prerequisite note: the 2026-07-12 exploration named the Shamir **reconstruction**
180	ceremony a hard prerequisite for removing the password escape hatch; both reconstruction
181	ceremonies (escrow-assisted and sovereign) have since landed (`share_recovery.rs`;
182	[identity-and-key-custody.md](../architecture/identity-and-key-custody.md), verified
183	2026-07-18), so that gate is satisfied.
184	
185	## Security invariants (all channels)
186	
187	- Wallet approval screen always shows client name, origin/redirect host, requested
188	  scopes, and requesting IP/geo before the biometric gate; approval is impossible

1	// The Notification Service Extension: the only place a sealed push is ever plaintext.
2	//
3	// A Custos instance HPKE-seals a notification to this device's key and hands it to a relay
4	// that holds the APNs key but no decryption key. The relay and Apple both carry the payload
5	// as opaque bytes beside a placeholder alert ("Custos / Encrypted notification"), and
6	// `mutable-content: 1` routes it here for the ~30 seconds iOS allows before it gives up and
7	// shows the placeholder.
8	//
9	// # The constraint that shapes everything below
10	//
11	// **An NSE cannot suppress an alert push.** If this code fails, times out, or declines to
12	// attach content, iOS displays the original payload anyway. So "drop what we cannot verify"
13	// is not on the menu; the only thing under this extension's control is *what the user reads*.
14	// The rule is therefore absolute: content that opened under HPKE Auth mode renders as
15	// content, and everything else renders as the explicit unverified notice. Never a guess,
16	// never a partial render, never the placeholder passed through as though it were news.
17	//
18	// That is what keeps a relay's junk push from being an impersonation. The relay can always
19	// generate noise — it holds the APNs key — but noise arrives labelled as unverifiable, which
20	// is detectable spam and grounds for switching relays, not a forged message from your server.
21	
22	import UserNotifications
23	
24	/// The decision the extension makes about one payload, split out from the `UNNotification`
25	/// machinery so every branch is reachable from a test.
26	enum NotifyOutcome: Equatable {
27	    case rendered(NotifyPayload)
28	    case unverified(NotifyFailureReason, kid: Int?)
29	}
30	
31	enum NotifyResolver {
32	    /// The user-visible copy for a payload this device cannot vouch for.
33	    ///
34	    /// Deliberately says what happened and nothing more. It names no sender ("from your
35	    /// Custos instance" is a category, not a claim about which one), states no cause the
36	    /// extension cannot know, and offers no action — the actionable version of this lives in
37	    /// Settings, where the breadcrumbs can say whether it happened once or twenty times.
38	    static let unverifiedTitle = "Unverified notification"
39	    static let unverifiedBody = "Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance."
40	
41	    /// Resolve an APNs `userInfo` into what should be shown.
42	    ///
43	    /// Pure over its inputs — the Keychain reads happen in the caller — so the whole failure
44	    /// ladder is exercisable on a simulator with no push and no registered key.
45	    static func resolve(
46	        userInfo: [AnyHashable: Any],
47	        recipientPrivateKey: Data?,
48	        pins: PinnedSenderKeys
49	    ) -> NotifyOutcome {
50	        guard let envelope = NotifyEnvelope.parse(userInfo: userInfo) else {
51	            return .unverified(.malformedPayload, kid: nil)
52	        }
53	        guard let recipientPrivateKey else {
54	            return .unverified(.keysUnavailable, kid: envelope.kid)
55	        }
56	
57	        let candidates = pins.candidates(for: envelope.kid)
58	        guard !candidates.isEmpty else {
59	            return .unverified(.unknownKid, kid: envelope.kid)
60	        }
61	
62	        // Try every key pinned under this `kid`. See `PinnedSenderKeys.candidates` for why
63	        // there can be more than one; Auth mode makes a wrong guess free.
64	        for didKey in candidates {
65	            guard let senderBytes = DidKey.p256PublicKeyBytes(from: didKey) else { continue }
66	            guard let plaintext = NotifyCrypto.open(
67	                recipientPrivateKey: recipientPrivateKey,
68	                senderPublicKey: senderBytes,
69	                encapsulatedKey: envelope.enc,
70	                ciphertext: envelope.ct
71	            ) else { continue }
72	
73	            // Past this point the payload is authenticated: only a holder of a pinned sender
74	            // private key could have produced it. A body we cannot parse is therefore our own
75	            // bug or a version skew, not an attack — but it still cannot be rendered as
76	            // content, because there is no content to render.
77	            guard let payload = NotifyPayload.decode(plaintext) else {
78	                return .unverified(.malformedPlaintext, kid: envelope.kid)
79	            }
80	            return .rendered(payload)
81	        }
82	
83	        return .unverified(.openFailed, kid: envelope.kid)
84	    }
85	}

87	final class NotificationService: UNNotificationServiceExtension {
88	    private var contentHandler: ((UNNotificationContent) -> Void)?
89	    private var bestAttempt: UNMutableNotificationContent?
90	
91	    override func didReceive(
92	        _ request: UNNotificationRequest,
93	        withContentHandler contentHandler: @escaping (UNNotificationContent) -> Void
94	    ) {
95	        self.contentHandler = contentHandler
96	        guard let content = request.content.mutableCopy() as? UNMutableNotificationContent else {
97	            // `UNNotificationContent.mutableCopy()` is documented to return the mutable class, so
98	            // this is a platform-contract violation rather than a state a payload can produce.
99	            // It still cannot be allowed to deliver `request.content`: that content is immutable,
100	            // so the sealed block cannot be stripped from it, and its title/body are the relay's
101	            // placeholder — the one combination the extension's rule forbids. A fresh content
102	            // carrying only the notice is the sole way to honour both halves here.
103	            //
104	            // No breadcrumb: the failure vocabulary describes payloads, and reporting this as a
105	            // payload problem would send the user looking at their keys for a bug in ours.
106	            contentHandler(Self.unverifiedContent())
107	            return
108	        }
109	        bestAttempt = content
110	
111	        let outcome = NotifyResolver.resolve(
112	            userInfo: request.content.userInfo,
113	            recipientPrivateKey: NotifyKeychain.read(
114	                account: NotifyKeychain.notificationKeyAccount
115	            ),
116	            pins: PinnedSenderKeys.parse(
117	                NotifyKeychain.read(account: NotifyKeychain.pinnedSenderKeysAccount)
118	            )
119	        )
120	
121	        switch outcome {
122	        case let .rendered(payload):
123	            content.title = payload.title
124	            content.body = payload.body
125	        case let .unverified(reason, kid):
126	            content.title = NotifyResolver.unverifiedTitle
127	            content.body = NotifyResolver.unverifiedBody
128	            NotifyBreadcrumbs.record(reason, kid: kid)
129	        }
130	
131	        Self.finish(content)
132	        contentHandler(content)
133	    }
134	
135	    /// iOS is about to give up on us.
136	    ///
137	    /// Whatever is in `bestAttempt` is delivered, so this path has to satisfy the same two
138	    /// obligations `didReceive` does — say "unverified" rather than let the relay's placeholder
139	    /// stand in for the server's words, and strip the sealed block. Neither gets an exception
140	    /// for running late: a timeout is the one route by which unstripped ciphertext, under a
141	    /// title the user reads as authentic, could reach the delivered-notification list.
142	    override func serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire() {
143	        guard let contentHandler, let bestAttempt else { return }
144	        // The presence of the sealed block IS the "we never finished" signal — `finish` strips it
145	        // and writes the notice in the same breath, so it can only still be here if resolution
146	        // was cut short. Testing that rather than the title keeps the two facts from drifting.
147	        if bestAttempt.userInfo[NotifyEnvelope.userInfoKey] != nil {
148	            bestAttempt.title = NotifyResolver.unverifiedTitle
149	            bestAttempt.body = NotifyResolver.unverifiedBody
150	        }
151	        Self.finish(bestAttempt)
152	        contentHandler(bestAttempt)
153	    }
154	
155	    /// The last thing done to any content that leaves this extension.
156	    ///
157	    /// The sealed block has served its purpose and must not ride along into the delivered
158	    /// notification, where the app — and anything reading `UNUserNotificationCenter`'s delivered
159	    /// list — would see ciphertext it has no use for. Factored out because "every exit path"
160	    /// is the actual requirement, and inlining it at each one is how an exit path gets missed.
161	    private static func finish(_ content: UNMutableNotificationContent) {
162	        content.userInfo.removeValue(forKey: NotifyEnvelope.userInfoKey)
163	    }
164	
165	    /// A fresh content carrying nothing but the unverified notice.
166	    ///
167	    /// For the exit where no mutable copy exists to strip, so substituting content is the only
168	    /// way to avoid delivering the sealed block.
169	    private static func unverifiedContent() -> UNMutableNotificationContent {
170	        let content = UNMutableNotificationContent()
171	        content.title = NotifyResolver.unverifiedTitle
172	        content.body = NotifyResolver.unverifiedBody
173	        return content
174	    }
175	}

1	// The pure half of the Notification Service Extension: everything that turns bytes into
2	// other bytes, with no Keychain, no CryptoKit, and no UserNotifications.
3	//
4	// It lives apart from NotificationService.swift for the same reason the wallet's Rust keeps
5	// `_impl` cores away from Tauri commands — this is the part an XCTest can drive on a
6	// simulator, and the part the Rust↔CryptoKit fixture cross-check exercises.
7	
8	import Foundation
9	
10	/// The `ezpds` object a sealed push carries beside its placeholder `aps` alert.
11	///
12	/// Wire shape (see `crates/notify-relay/src/protocol.rs`):
13	/// `{ "v": 1, "kid": 3, "enc": "<b64url>", "ct": "<b64url>" }`
14	struct NotifyEnvelope: Equatable {
15	    /// Protocol version. Only `1` is understood; anything else is a payload sealed by a
16	    /// newer instance for a newer extension, and must render as unverified rather than be
17	    /// guessed at.
18	    static let supportedVersion = 1
19	
20	    /// The `userInfo` key the sealed block travels under. Named once because it is used for two
21	    /// opposite purposes — reading the envelope, and *removing* it before delivery — and a typo
22	    /// in the second would leak ciphertext into the delivered-notification list silently.
23	    static let userInfoKey = "ezpds"
24	
25	    let version: Int
26	    /// The instance-scoped sender-key id. Not a global identifier: two Custos instances both
27	    /// start their `kid` sequence at 1, which is why the pin store is keyed by host and every
28	    /// candidate under this id is tried.
29	    let kid: Int
30	    /// HPKE encapsulated key — 65 raw bytes for DHKEM(P-256).
31	    let enc: Data
32	    /// AEAD ciphertext with the 16-byte AES-GCM tag appended.
33	    let ct: Data
34	
35	    /// Read the envelope out of an APNs `userInfo` dictionary.
36	    ///
37	    /// Returns `nil` for anything that is not a well-formed v1 envelope — a junk push from a
38	    /// misbehaving relay, a `content-available` ping, or a future version. The caller renders
39	    /// all of those identically (the unverified notice), so this deliberately does not
40	    /// distinguish "absent" from "malformed": neither is content this device can vouch for.
41	    static func parse(userInfo: [AnyHashable: Any]) -> NotifyEnvelope? {
42	        guard let block = userInfo[userInfoKey] as? [String: Any],
43	              let version = block["v"] as? Int,
44	              version == supportedVersion,
45	              let kid = block["kid"] as? Int,
46	              let encText = block["enc"] as? String,
47	              let ctText = block["ct"] as? String,
48	              let enc = Data(base64URLEncoded: encText),
49	              let ct = Data(base64URLEncoded: ctText),
50	              !enc.isEmpty, !ct.isEmpty
51	        else { return nil }
52	
53	        return NotifyEnvelope(version: version, kid: kid, enc: enc, ct: ct)
54	    }
55	}

57	/// The decrypted plaintext a Custos instance seals.
58	///
59	/// Wire shape: `{ "type": …, "title": …, "body": …, "data": { … }, "pad": "…" }`. `pad` is
60	/// dropped on the floor here — its whole job was to make the *serialized APNs request* land
61	/// on a padding bucket, which is finished by the time these bytes exist.
62	struct NotifyPayload: Equatable, Decodable {
63	    let type: String
64	    let title: String
65	    let body: String
66	
67	    /// Decode sealed plaintext, rejecting a payload with nothing to render.
68	    ///
69	    /// An empty title *and* body would produce a banner indistinguishable from a silent
70	    /// delivery failure, so it is treated as a malformed payload and rendered as the
71	    /// unverified notice instead — the extension's one rule is that it never shows something
72	    /// it cannot stand behind.
73	    static func decode(_ plaintext: Data) -> NotifyPayload? {
74	        guard let payload = try? JSONDecoder().decode(NotifyPayload.self, from: plaintext),
75	              !(payload.title.isEmpty && payload.body.isEmpty)
76	        else { return nil }
77	        return payload
78	    }

81	// MARK: - base64url
82	
83	extension Data {
84	    /// Decode unpadded base64url — the encoding every binary field in the envelope uses
85	    /// (`URL_SAFE_NO_PAD` on the Rust side). Foundation only speaks standard base64 with
86	    /// padding, so translate the alphabet and re-pad.
87	    init?(base64URLEncoded input: String) {
88	        var text = input.replacingOccurrences(of: "-", with: "+")
89	            .replacingOccurrences(of: "_", with: "/")
90	        let remainder = text.count % 4
91	        if remainder == 1 {
92	            // 4n+1 is not a length any base64 encoding can produce; padding it would
93	            // manufacture a decodable string out of corrupt input.
94	            return nil
95	        }
96	        if remainder > 0 {
97	            text += String(repeating: "=", count: 4 - remainder)
98	        }
99	        guard let decoded = Data(base64Encoded: text) else { return nil }
100	        self = decoded
101	    }
102	}

104	// MARK: - did:key
105	
106	/// Decode a P-256 `did:key` into its raw SEC1 public-key bytes.
107	///
108	/// The pinned sender keys arrive from Custos as `did:key:z…` strings and are stored verbatim
109	/// by the wallet (`notifications.rs`), so the extension has to undo the encoding itself:
110	/// multibase base58btc (`z` prefix) wrapping the multicodec varint `0x1200` — written
111	/// little-endian-base128 as `0x80 0x24` — followed by a 33-byte compressed point.
112	///
113	/// Returns `nil` for anything that is not exactly that. A sender key this device cannot
114	/// decode is simply not a candidate; HPKE Auth mode would fail closed on it anyway, so
115	/// skipping costs nothing and misreading could not gain anything.
116	enum DidKey {
117	    /// The multicodec prefix for `p256-pub`, varint-encoded.
118	    static let p256Prefix: [UInt8] = [0x80, 0x24]
119	    /// A compressed SEC1 P-256 point: 1 tag byte + 32-byte X.
120	    static let compressedPointLength = 33
121	
122	    static func p256PublicKeyBytes(from didKey: String) -> Data? {
123	        guard didKey.hasPrefix("did:key:z") else { return nil }
124	        let multibase = String(didKey.dropFirst("did:key:z".count))
125	        guard let decoded = Base58.decode(multibase),
126	              decoded.count == p256Prefix.count + compressedPointLength,
127	              Array(decoded.prefix(p256Prefix.count)) == p256Prefix
128	        else { return nil }
129	        return Data(decoded.dropFirst(p256Prefix.count))
130	    }
131	}
132	
133	/// base58btc, the one multibase alphabet `did:key` uses.
134	///
135	/// Hand-rolled because the extension links nothing but system frameworks: a Swift package
136	/// dependency in an NSE is a second supply chain in the one target that runs on a locked
137	/// screen, for ~30 lines of long division.
138	enum Base58 {
139	    private static let alphabet = Array("REDACTED".utf8)
140	
141	    static func decode(_ input: String) -> [UInt8]? {
142	        var bytes: [UInt8] = [0]
143	        for character in input.utf8 {
144	            guard let value = alphabet.firstIndex(of: character) else { return nil }
145	            var carry = value
146	            for index in bytes.indices.reversed() {
147	                carry += 58 * Int(bytes[index])
148	                bytes[index] = UInt8(carry & 0xff)
149	                carry >>= 8
150	            }
151	            while carry > 0 {
152	                bytes.insert(UInt8(carry & 0xff), at: 0)
153	                carry >>= 8
154	            }
155	        }
156	        // Every leading '1' encodes one leading zero byte, which the arithmetic above cannot
157	        // recover (it carries no magnitude).
158	        var leadingZeros = 0
159	        for character in input.utf8 {
160	            guard character == alphabet[0] else { break }
161	            leadingZeros += 1
162	        }
163	        // Drop the seed byte and any zeros the long division introduced, then restore the
164	        // encoded ones.
165	        let significant = Array(bytes.drop(while: { $0 == 0 }))
166	        return Array(repeating: 0, count: leadingZeros) + significant
167	    }
168	}

2	
3	Last verified: 2026-07-27
4	
5	## Purpose
6	
7	Swift that belongs to the iOS apps but to neither app's Rust crate. Today that is exactly one
8	thing: the wallet's **Notification Service Extension**, which unseals encrypted push
9	notifications on arrival.
10	
11	It sits at the repo root rather than under `apps/identity-wallet/` for the same reason
12	`scripts/ios/` does — the XcodeGen template that compiles it is shared by both apps, so its
13	inputs are shared too. The operator console will grow an extension from these same sources when it
14	adopts notifications.
15	
16	## Contracts
17	
18	### `NotificationService/` — the extension (`{{app.name}}_NSE`)
19	
20	**Exposes:** `NotificationService`, a `UNNotificationServiceExtension` subclass iOS
21	instantiates via `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` when a push carries `mutable-content: 1`.
22	
23	**Guarantees:**
24	- A payload that opens under HPKE Auth mode renders as content. **Everything else renders as
25	  the explicit unverified notice** — never a guess, never a partial render, never the relay's
26	  placeholder passed through as though it were news. This is the extension's single rule, and
27	  it holds on the timeout path too (`serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire`).
28	- The sealed `ezpds` block is stripped from the delivered notification, so ciphertext never
29	  reaches the app's delivered-notification list.
30	- Every failure leaves a breadcrumb in the shared Keychain, best effort. A Keychain that will
31	  not take a diagnostic never costs the user the notice itself.
32	
33	**Expects:**
34	- `keychain-access-groups` listing `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared` **first**
35	  (`apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist`). Nothing here names an access group
36	  in a query — naming one would mean discovering `AppIdentifierPrefix` at runtime, on the one
37	  code path that must work on a locked screen — so the entitlement's *order* is the mechanism.
38	- The wallet having registered: `notification-key-priv` and `notification-sender-keys`, both
39	  under `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, written by `notifications.rs`.
40	- iOS 17. `HPKE.Recipient`'s auth-mode initializer does not exist before it.
41	
42	| File | What it holds |
43	|---|---|
44	| `NotificationService.swift` | The `UNNotificationServiceExtension` shell, plus `NotifyResolver` — the pure failure ladder every branch of which is a banner someone reads |
45	| `NotifyCrypto.swift` | CryptoKit `HPKE.Recipient` in auth mode, suite/`info`/`aad` pinned to `crates/crypto/src/hpke.rs` |
46	| `NotifyEnvelope.swift` | Envelope + payload parsing, base64url, `did:key` → SEC1, base58 |
47	| `NotifyKeychain.swift` | The shared-Keychain reads, and the pin document's shape |
48	| `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` | The bounded failure log the app surfaces in Settings |
49	
50	### `NotificationServiceTests/` — the logic-test bundle (`{{app.name}}_NSETests`)
51	
52	Compiled with the extension's sources rather than linking them: an app extension has no
53	testable module to import, since there is no `TEST_HOST` an extension can be loaded into.
54	
55	`NotifyFixtureTests` is the **cross-implementation check** — it opens
56	`crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json` (sealed by Rust's `hpke` crate) with
57	CryptoKit. RFC 9180's appendix carries no vector for this suite, so nothing else proves the two
58	agree on the pinned suite, the `info` string, the empty `aad`, and the key encodings. The
59	fixture is referenced **in place** by the template — there is no copy here to drift.
60	
61	## Dependencies
62	
63	System frameworks only: CryptoKit, Foundation, Security, UserNotifications. Deliberately no
64	Swift package dependency — a package in the extension is a second supply chain in the one
65	process that runs on a locked screen.
66	
67	## Key Decisions
68	
69	- **Swift, not a second Rust staticlib.** Decryption is ~200 lines of CryptoKit; a second
70	  staticlib would double the iOS build's slowest step for it.
71	- **Breadcrumbs go to the shared Keychain, not an app-group container.** The keychain group is
72	  already entitled and needs no Apple Developer portal work; an app group would be a second new
73	  entitlement on both bundles. The cost is that a push arriving before the first unlock after a
74	  reboot leaves no breadcrumb — the one failure that repairs itself, and the least worth
75	  recording.
76	- **The extension is gated to the wallet's bundle id** in `scripts/ios/project.yml`. An app
77	  extension is a separate bundle needing its own App ID, profile, and signing secret; rendering
78	  one for admin-companion would cost a second set of those for an extension that cannot decrypt
79	  anything until the console has a shared keychain group and registered notification keys of its own.
80	
81	## Invariants
82	
83	- The Keychain service name, account names, and both JSON document shapes in
84	  `NotifyKeychain.swift` / `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` are **copies** of constants in
85	  `apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/{keychain,notifications}.rs`. Two separate bundles can
86	  only agree by both spelling the same strings; a rename on one side is silent on the other.
87	- `PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME` is pinned to `NotificationService` in the template. It is half of
88	  `NSExtensionPrincipalClass`, so a drift leaves iOS unable to instantiate the extension — a
89	  failure indistinguishable from a push that never arrived. `just ios-check` greps the pbxproj
90	  for it.
91	- The failure `reason` vocabulary (`NotifyFailureReason`) is shared with the app's
92	  `NotificationFailure.reason` and the frontend's `NotificationFailureReason`. Both readers
93	  tolerate an unrecognized value on purpose: the extension versions independently, and the entry
94	  a strict reader would drop is the one the user is asking about. A new case still needs wording
95	  in `apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/notification-health.ts`.
96	- CI gates, in order of what they can catch:
97	  - `just _nse-typecheck` (macOS, part of `just ios-pr-check`) — `swiftc -typecheck` of the
98	    extension's sources, then of the test bundle exactly as the template composes it, against
99	    the real iOS SDK at the deployment target both apps declare. No simulator, no signing, no
100	    generated Xcode project. This is the only thing that compiles this Swift before a release
101	    archive would.
102	  - `just ios-template-check` (Linux) — target present, gated to the wallet, embedded,
103	    principal class and module name, entitlements order and least privilege, sources exist.
104	  - `just ios-check` (macOS) — the same structural facts in the generated pbxproj.
105	  Nothing *runs* the tests in CI: `ios-pr-check` performs no `xcodebuild`, so the fixture
106	  cross-check is a local `xcodebuild test -scheme <app>_NSETests` (or `⌘U` on that scheme).

Obsign now reads the encrypted notifications your Custos instance sends. Until now your phone could receive one but not open it, so every notification arrived as a placeholder; a small extension bundled with the app now unseals each one the moment it arrives — on the lock screen, without waking the app, and without the relay in the middle or Apple ever seeing the text. What you read is what your server wrote.

When a notification *cannot* be opened, Obsign says so plainly rather than showing you something that looks genuine. iOS does not let an app silently discard a notification, so anything that fails to unseal — a relay sending noise, a message signed with a key your phone has not seen, or one arriving before you have unlocked your phone since restarting it — appears as an explicit "Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance". It is never dressed up as real content, which is what stops whoever carries your notifications from being able to put words in your server's mouth.

Because that notice on its own cannot tell you *which* of those happened, Settings gains a Notifications section that can. It counts the recent failures and names the likely cause in plain language — and, where there is something to do, says what: a key mismatch is usually fixed by opening one of your identities, since Obsign refreshes the keys on every contact with your server, while a run of unrecognisable notifications points at the relay rather than at anything of yours being at risk. Once you have dealt with it, you can clear the record so the next real report is not lost in an old one.

Signing in to an app can now come to you. When a sign-in page knows which account it is for, your Custos instance sends a sealed push to Obsign; tapping it opens the approval screen directly on that request — no code to type, no QR to scan. The push travels the same encrypted path as every Obsign notification: the relay carries an opaque sealed payload and an opaque delivery handle, so neither it nor Apple ever learns that a login is happening, for whom, or from where. And Obsign only acts on a tapped notification it could cryptographically verify came from your instance.

Because a prompt that finds *you* is exactly where tap-fatigue attacks live, approval on this channel demands one extra proof: the sign-in page shows a two-digit number, and Obsign requires you to type it before Face ID. If someone else started that login, you are not looking at their screen, so there is nothing you can type — a blind "Approve" is impossible, and your server enforces the number, not just the app. A wrong number never kills the request; denying it (which needs no number) does, and is exactly the right answer to a prompt you did not start.

If the push never arrives — notifications off, relay down, a new phone — nothing is lost: the same sign-in page still shows the typed code and the QR, and either one opens the same request in Obsign, where the number is still asked for and still on the page in front of you.

Wallet-confirmed OAuth consent Phase C: push-to-approve with mandatory number matching

Push adds a delivery path onto the Phase A pending-authorization primitive —
nothing about the signed envelope or the completion tail changes.

Server (Custos):
- V060: match_code + push_dispatched_at on pending_oauth_authorizations
  (single-use latch; derived-status doctrine)
- GET /oauth/authorize's wallet path dispatches a sealed `login-approval`
  push when the login_hint names a hosted account — resolved with LOCAL
  lookups only (the hint is attacker-suppliable on an unauthenticated
  surface) — via the existing notify pipeline; notify_device now reports
  the enqueued count so the number-match requirement latches only when a
  push actually went out
- The consent page displays the two-digit match number; the wallet preview
  reports matchRequired; /oauth/authorize/approve refuses an approval whose
  matchCode doesn't match (403, request left pending for a retype) —
  checked server-side after signature/authority verification, outside the
  envelope. Denials never require the number.
- New push_dispatched audit event; loopback e2e proves the sealed payload
  opens on-device, carries no code field, and the relay/Apple see only the
  fixed placeholder

NSE (ios/NotificationService):
- Verified payloads may carry allowlisted routing identifiers
  (data.requestId/did); they survive into the delivered notification as
  the ezpdsRoute userInfo block — written only on the HPKE-verified path,
  so its presence is itself the authenticity statement

Wallet (Obsign):
- apns.rs gains the notification-tap callback (add-only class_addMethod,
  UNUserNotificationCenter delegate) feeding the new host-tested
  notification_routes slot + notification_route event
- +page.svelte routes a tapped login-approval into the consent approval
  screen on its request_id (managed-DID-gated, interruptible-surface-gated;
  drain-on-mount covers cold start, the event covers warm foreground)
- OAuthConsentApprovalScreen: initialRequestId entry + the number-match
  checkpoint before the biometric gate (type-the-number, GitHub style —
  decided over select-from-three: typing leaves no guess-tap surface);
  MATCH_CODE_MISMATCH keeps the review open for a retype

Docs: design plan Phase C landed note + number-format decision, AGENTS.md
updates, bruno request/response docs, regenerated IPC reference,
changelog fragment.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
